n: Essential Clinical Anatomy for Ward Rounds

faq.a: Irritation of the diaphragm transmits pain via the phrenic nerve to the C3‑C5 dermatomes (shoulder tip).
faq.q: Why does gallbladder disease present with right shoulder pain?

faq.a: X‑ray shows air‑fluid levels but may miss partial obstruction; clinical assessment and ultrasound are essential where CT is unavailable.
faq.q: Can you rely on plain X‑ray for diagnosing intestinal obstruction?

faq.a: Pain and inspiratory arrest on palpation of the RUQ during deep breath suggests gallbladder inflammation.
faq.q: What is the significance of a positive Murphy’s sign?

exam: A 22‑year‑old with RLQ pain, fever and guarding — which anatomical structure is most likely inflamed and why? — Appendicitis; location at the confluence of the teniae coli, supplied by the appendicular artery.

A patient with sickle cell disease presents with left flank pain and hematuria — what organ is involved and what is the pathophysiology? — Left kidney; vaso‑occlusive infarction causing papillary necrosis.

During a trauma survey you find a tender, rigid abdomen but no external wounds — what is your next immediate step? — Assume intra‑abdominal bleeding; arrange urgent laparotomy or transfer to surgical facility.
How does malaria‑related hepatomegaly alter physical examination findings? — Enlarged, smooth liver edge palpable >2 cm below costal margin; may cause RUQ fullness without tenderness.

A pregnant woman in labour has a palpable mass in the LUQ — what differential diagnoses should you consider? — Enlarged spleen (malaria, schistosomiasis), left renal cyst, or uterine fundal enlargement; assess with ultrasound if possible.

Why is the presence of shifting dullness more reliable than static dullness in diagnosing ascites? — Fluid moves with patient position, creating a dependent dull area and a superior resonant area, confirming free fluid.

Explain why a high‑pitched, tympanic percussion note over the abdomen suggests intestinal obstruction. — Accumulated gas in dilated loops produces tympany; helps differentiate from solid organ enlargement.

In a low‑resource setting without CT, how would you differentiate between perforated peptic ulcer and acute pancreatitis? — Look for sudden severe epigastric pain with rigid abdomen and free air on upright X‑ray (perforation) versus persistent epigastric pain radiating to back with elevated serum amylase if available (pancreatitis).
ai.title: Essential Clinical Anatomy for Ward Rounds
ai.subject: Anatomy
ai.summary: A concise review of clinically relevant anatomy focusing on surface landmarks, organ relations, blood and nerve supply, and common injuries. Tailored for low‑resource settings where imaging may be limited.

b: Surface landmarks correlate with underlying viscera.
Anatomical variations are common in African populations.
sections.p: Understanding the layout of the torso allows rapid localisation of pain, organ dysfunction and trauma, guiding history, examination and urgent decisions.

b: Right upper quadrant (RUQ): liver, gallbladder, right kidney, duodenum.
Left upper quadrant (LUQ): spleen, stomach, left kidney, tail of pancreas.
Right lower quadrant (RLQ): appendix, cecum, right ovary/fallopian tube.
Left lower quadrant (LLQ): sigmoid colon, left ovary/fallopian tube.
sections.p: The abdomen is divided into nine regions and four quadrants; key organs include liver, spleen, stomach, duodenum, pancreas, kidneys and large intestine.

b: Peritoneal cavity communicates freely between quadrants.
Retroperitoneal organs (kidneys, pancreas) are fixed to posterior abdominal wall.
sections.p: Organs are bounded by peritoneal reflections and fascial planes that dictate spread of infection or fluid.

b: Celiac trunk supplies liver, stomach, spleen.
Superior mesenteric artery supplies small intestine and right colon.
Inferior mesenteric artery supplies left colon and rectum.
sections.p: Arterial inflow follows the aortic branches; venous drainage mirrors arterial supply via portal and systemic veins.

b: Phrenic nerve irritation causes shoulder tip pain (Kehr's sign).
Iliohypogastric and ilioinguinal nerves supply lower abdominal wall.
sections.p: Visceral pain is transmitted by autonomic fibers to spinal segments T5‑L1; somatic pain follows thoracolumbar nerves.

b: Liver detoxifies drugs and produces clotting factors.
Spleen filters blood and mounts immune response.
sections.p: The abdomen houses digestion, absorption, immune surveillance (gut‑associated lymphoid tissue) and excretion.

b: RUQ pain with fever → hepatitis, malaria‑related hepatomegaly, or biliary sepsis.
RLQ tenderness with guarding → appendicitis or tubal rupture.
Flank dullness and costovertebral angle tenderness → pyelonephritis or renal abscess.
sections.p: Trauma, infection and obstructive disease present with characteristic patterns that can be inferred from anatomy.

t.b: Identifies organ‑specific tenderness, guarding, rebound and organomegaly; guides need for imaging or urgent surgery.
Answers whether fluid collection is intra‑abdominal or retroperitoneal; if unavailable, use bedside percussion and shifting dullness.

b: Percuss liver edge: dullness extending >2 cm below the right costal margin suggests hepatomegaly.
Shifted dullness on supine patient indicates ascites; tap the dependent flank for fluid.
Ask patient to point to maximal pain; correlate with quadrant anatomy.
sections.p: Key bedside tricks help compensate for limited investigations.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with hypotension or tachycardia
Signs of peritonitis (rigid abdomen, rebound tenderness)
Rapidly expanding abdominal mass or pulsatile mass
